"3 reasons why we are living in a simulation"

I never understood why people allude to the potential simulation's controllers as being some super-distant super-alien species.

For one contrary hypothetical, it's quite clear that immersive simulations will offer some of the most phenomenal methods of education. And we live in a time that's somewhat interesting for a couple of reasons. It's one of the first with an incredibly extensive digital record. Organizations like the NSA are doing a tremendous service to historians of the future and the military as well as companies like Google are already starting to map every single inch of the planet in extensive detail. In other words we're living in one of the first eras where a truly immersive "set" could genuinely be created.

Another interesting coincidence is how uncommonly important the era we're living in is. Most of us have lived through the birth of the internet which is something that will stay with our species for as long as it exists. And we're living in an era where we will almost certainly also see humanity first begin to make strides onto another planet as well as the advent of major automation of labor. This era, which we're all living in, is going to be a sharp 'junction' point in the history of our species.

I think the above arguments pale in comparison to the mathematical argument, but they're again just interesting coincidences. For all you know you're taking part in a 30 minute edutainment simulator on humanity's first steps beyond its own planet being given in the not too distant future. Give some millions or billions of people genuine roles with a given backstory and they're generally going to play out in a way unlikely to change things too much. Add some filler AI that ensures the main storyline plays out as it should and you're set to go. Great entertainment and great education all in one.

Perhaps one major argument against this again goes back to the mathematical argument of the simulation hypothesis. This argument begins tying a specific simulation to some notion of "reality" when again all we can really know is that there would be some number of simulations across an infinite possibilities of time, and only one real reality. Tying any given simulation back to reality and time in any specific way is arguably no more justified than arguing that we live in the one original "real" universe and time.
Simulation theory is like string theory. Internally consistent, able to explain some phenomena, impossible to prove (and ultimately useless).
